newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels hold firm despite signs of optimism.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels hold firm despite signs of optimism.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 83 VIP hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima held out for a 13th day on Monday despite signs of progress following their first direct contact with the government.
The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas placed three signs in an upper window of the residence spelling out the reasons for their continued stand.
The signs read: "Our prisoners do not receive the same humane treatment - MRTA"; "Social fighters also deserve freedom - MRTA"; and "The people want peace with social justice - MRTA".

The messages underscored a more conciliatory stance by the rebels in recent days, angling more for improved conditions for jailed comrades and recognition of their movement as opposed to earlier demands for the release of all their prisoners and sweeping changes to Peru's economic system.
Rebel leader Nestor Cerpa met on Saturday for more than three hours with President Alberto Fujimori's designated mediator Education Minister Domingo Palermo inside the besieged residence.

The face-to-face meeting, the first between the two sides, brought immediate results: the release of 20 more hostages, bringing to over 420 the number of captives freed since the rebels stormed a lavish reception at the residence on Dec 17.

Palermo said following the release of the hostages -- mostly Peruvian diplomats and Japanese businessmen -- that there had been "advances for the solution of this serious incident", but gave no details.
And in a statement read out by one of the newly freed hostages, the MRTA expressed a willingness "to withdraw from the occupied residence by way of dialogue."
The communique made no mention of their main condition -- the release of around 400 jailed comrades -- nor an earlier threat to kill the hostages if their demands were not met.
The meeting was greeted as a breakthrough by International Committee of the Red Cross mediator Michel Minnig, who until Saturday had been the main contact between the residence and the outside world.
"A threshold has been crossed with the establishment of direct communication between the government and the Tupac Amaru. This is a positive step," he said in an interview with Swiss television.

But Saturday's apparently significant developments were followed by a day of inactivity. No more hostages were released and Red Cross officials were the only outsiders to enter the building. They brought 110 rations of food, including 20 for diabetics, and candles for the 10 lanterns which have provided the only light since fuel for a power generator ran out over a week ago.

Minnig warned that Saturday's events did not guarantee an early end to the crisis. "The fact that members of the guerrilla group and representatives of the government met does not mean the problem is simple," he said. "It means that discussions are starting and disagreement is still there."
Echoing the new mood, the MRTA's international spokesman, Isaac Velazco, told Reuters on Sunday the rebels were ready to negotiate their original demand to free all jailed comrades.

"We still insist on the liberation of the political prisoners, but we consider that an intermediate solution can be reached," he said in an interview from Hamburg. Asked what that meant, he said: "Not necessarily the liberation of all the political prisoners."
In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto welcomed the new developments but warned against over-optimism.
"It is not time yet to get our hopes up but reading the guerrillas' demands, it seems possible to have a dialogue with the rebels," he told reporters.
Hasimoto received a letter from the nine Japanese nationals freed which expressed fears about conditions for those left inside.
But Minnig said: "Medically the situation of the people is under control. Right now the situation is quiet. They are trying to have normal lives."
Freed hostages have said the roughly 20 heavily armed MRTA rebels have booby-trapped and mined the residence against possible attack.
The guerrillas still held a range of top Peruvian government officials and military officers, about 20 Japanese businessmen and diplomats, three ambassadors and the brother of President Fujimori.
